paras: The killing of Sandy Bynum was the fatal shooting of a Black Republican leader by Thomas G. Hewlett, a former U.S. deputy marshal, at a political barbecue at Ayer's Spring near Huntsville, Alabama, on August 5, 1882. Hewlett fled on horseback, was later tried for second-degree murder, and was acquitted. Telegraphed across the country, the killing became a talking point in the partisan press over political violence in the South.

Bynum was described by the wire as the most prominent leader of the Republicans in Madison County, and he was a speaker for the Independent ticket in the August election campaign. A Huntsville letter said he had held a post in Washington under Grant, while the Huntsville Independent called him a "notorious colored gambler." Hewlett was opposing the Independent ticket, and the Savannah Morning News described him as a white Republican officeholder who had recently lost his place.

According to eyewitnesses who rode to the barbecue with Bynum, Hewlett passed their hack on the Triana road on Saturday morning, and soon after arriving Bynum was told that Hewlett was abusing him to a group standing apart from the main crowd. Bynum went over, and Hewlett told him that if he made personal allusions to him in his speech he would kill him; both men swore, and each denied carrying pistols. As Hewlett turned as if to leave, he wheeled with a pistol and fired, striking Bynum in the breast, then fired twice more as Bynum walked away stooping, and Bynum fell dead.

The Huntsville Independent gave a similar account, adding that some said Hewlett had sent for Bynum and that the shots struck the breast, the ear and an arm. A Huntsville letter quoted an eyewitness who said Hewlett opened the exchange and that Bynum was unarmed, but it added that other accounts had Bynum abusing Hewlett for several days and moments before the shooting.

Cries of "Shoot him" and "Kill him" rose from the crowd, which the Gazette's witnesses put at six to seven hundred men, and leading white and Black men urged that the law take its course. Hewlett reloaded his revolver, held off the crowd with two pistols, and, according to the Independent, offered to surrender to the sheriff but not to give up his arms before riding toward the Tennessee River.

The first wire reported a rumor that Hewlett had been arrested that night, a claim some digests later printed as fact, while the Gazette said a week later that his whereabouts were unknown. On August 8 the Central Republican Arthur Club met at the U.S. court room and unanimously adopted resolutions declaring that Bynum had been "mercilessly murdered" and extending sympathy to his wife and children.

Hewlett was tried in the Madison County circuit court before Judge Speake on an indictment for murder in the second degree, with about fifty witnesses sworn for both sides. After counsel waived argument, the jury stayed out overnight and on the morning of September 2 returned a verdict of "Not Guilty," and the court discharged Hewlett.

The Huntsville wire ran in papers from St. Paul to Salt Lake City, with the New-York Tribune heading it "A Republican Negro Murdered" and the St. Paul Daily Globe "A Southern 'Outrage.'" Condensed versions garbled the facts: some made Hewlett a sitting deputy or a U.S. marshal, and the Maysville Evening Bulletin and the Eaton Democrat reversed the roles, reporting that Bynum had killed Hewlett.

Republican papers treated the shooting as political murder, with the Wheeling Intelligencer heading its letter "The Alabama Plan" and the Belmont Chronicle calling it an example of "political intolerance" against a leader "whose influence was feared." The Democratic New Hampshire Patriot allowed that the killing "may have been justifiable" and accused Republicans of a double standard, while the Savannah Morning News mocked Northern "Radical" papers on learning that the killer was a white Republican.

In Huntsville the Gazette printed the eyewitness story under the heading "Ayer's Springs Tragedy" alongside the club's resolutions, while the Huntsville Independent's account, headed "A Polite Murderer" in reprints, described Hewlett doffing his hat to the crowd as he rode away.

The wire placed the killing at Huntsville on August 5, two briefs gave August 6, and the National Republican said Saturday night, but the club resolutions and the local accounts place it at Ayer's Spring by day on August 5. Accounts also differ over who sought the confrontation, though all of the fuller reports agree that Hewlett drew and fired.

reader.title: Killing of Sandy Bynum
bases: A single former deputy marshal, not acting in any reported official capacity, shot Bynum after a quarrel at a political barbecue; no mob, posse, arrest or custody is involved (A43, A52, A7).

The Huntsville wire, two separate local accounts (the Gazette's eyewitnesses and the Huntsville Independent), the Arthur Club resolutions and the trial report agree that Hewlett shot and killed Bynum at the Ayer's Spring rally; two briefs that reverse the roles are contradicted by all of them (A7, A43, A52, A42, A54, A28, A35).

accounts.label: Huntsville wire
accounts.gist: Hewlett shot and killed Bynum at an Independent rally; a crowd of Black men vowed to kill Hewlett and was pacified with difficulty; Hewlett fled and was rumored arrested.

accounts.label: Eyewitnesses who rode with Bynum (Huntsville Gazette)
accounts.gist: Told Hewlett was abusing him, Bynum went over; Hewlett threatened to kill him if he made personal allusions in his speech, both swore, and Hewlett wheeled and fired, hitting Bynum in the breast and twice more as he walked away.

accounts.label: Huntsville Independent
accounts.gist: Some said Hewlett sent for Bynum; after mutual cursing Hewlett fired three balls, reloaded on a log, offered to surrender to the sheriff without giving up his arms, and rode off toward the Tennessee River.

accounts.label: Huntsville letter (Wheeling Intelligencer)
accounts.gist: An eyewitness said Hewlett confronted the unarmed Bynum and fired three times; other accounts said Bynum had been abusive of Hewlett for days and just before the shooting.

framing.detail: New-York Tribune headline 'A Republican Negro Murdered'; Wheeling Intelligencer 'The Alabama Plan. Cowardly Murder at a Political Meeting'.
Belmont Chronicle editorial treats it as political intolerance, the assailant 'picking a quarrel with his defenseless victim'.
New Hampshire Patriot (Democratic) says the killing 'may have been justifiable' and accuses Republicans of a double standard.
Savannah Morning News mocks Northern 'Radical' papers, noting the killer was a white Republican.
Dozens of papers ran the Huntsville wire or digest versions, some reversing killer and victim.
